hook.line: Vale's mother says nobody in Medellín makes desserts like her daughter. In Colombia a person who is excellent at something is a *duro*, a hard one.
hook.es: Vale es una dura para los postres.
hook.en: Vale is a real pro at desserts.

examples.es: Es una dura para las matemáticas.
examples.en: She is a whiz at math.

examples.es: Mi hermano es un duro para el fútbol.
examples.en: My brother is brilliant at soccer.

examples.es: Don Hernando era un duro para manejar.
examples.en: Don Hernando was a real pro at driving.

examples.en: Mariana is a whiz at writing.

examples.es: Tomás no es un duro para las cuentas.
examples.en: Tomás is no whiz at sums.

examples.es: Eres un duro para los idiomas.
examples.en: You are a whiz at languages. (to a man, informal)

rule:
To say someone is excellent at something, use *ser un duro* for a man or *ser una dura* for a woman, then *para* and the skill: *es una dura para las matemáticas*.

The noun matches the person, not the skill. A group is *unos duros*.

Watch out: *es duro* with no *un* just means "it is hard". English says "a whiz" or "a pro"; Spanish says "a hard one".

To praise a friend, *un crack* also works everywhere.
smallPrint: Teachers call *duro* here a noun made from an adjective. It is Colombian; in Spain you would hear *un hacha* or *un fiera*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick the right form and type the whole sentence: *Mi hermana es ___ para el fútbol.* (un duro or una dura)
yourTurn.answer: Mi hermana es una dura para el fútbol.
yourTurn.why: *Hermana* is a woman, so the noun is *una dura*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: She is a whiz at math.
yourTurn.answer: Es una dura para las matemáticas.
accept: Ella es una dura para las matemáticas.
yourTurn.why: A woman is *una dura*, then *para* and the skill.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: My brother is brilliant at soccer.
yourTurn.answer: Mi hermano es un duro para el fútbol.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Don Hernando was a real pro at driving.
yourTurn.answer: Don Hernando era un duro para manejar.
yourTurn.why: *Era* puts it in the past, and after *para* you can use a verb as well as a noun.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Tomás es un duro para las cuentas.* Say: Tomás is no whiz at sums.
yourTurn.answer: Tomás no es un duro para las cuentas.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it to a group: *Eres un duro para los idiomas.* Say: You all are whizzes at languages.
yourTurn.answer: Ustedes son unos duros para los idiomas.
yourTurn.why: For *ustedes* use *son* and the plural *unos duros*.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a friend (a man): Are you a whiz at math?
accept: ¿Tú eres un duro para las matemáticas?
yourTurn.why: To a man, *un duro*; the question keeps the same words.

pitfalls.wrong: Es una duro para las matemáticas.
pitfalls.right: Es una dura para las matemáticas.
pitfalls.why: Almost. The noun has to match the person, so a woman is *una dura*.

pitfalls.right: Es una dura para las matemáticas.
pitfalls.why: Almost. Without *un* or *una*, *es duro* means that something is hard, not that someone is good.

pitfalls.wrong: Es un duro de las matemáticas.
pitfalls.right: Es un duro para las matemáticas.

personal: Say who is a *duro* or a *dura* at something among people you know, with *es un duro para…* or *es una dura para…*.
